entries.730d87828ca0c4b7462b411845e1f1ec45226f41: <div sID="gen33590" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="2Pet.3" sID="2Pet.3"/> <div eID="gen33590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33591" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33592" type="x-p"/> The apostle drawing towards the conclusion of his second epistle, begins this last chapter with repeating the account of his design and scope in writing a second time to them, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.1-2Pet.3.2">ver. 1-2</reference>. II. He proceeds to mention one thing that induced him to write this second epistle, namely, the coming of scoffers, whom he describes, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3-2Pet.3.7">ver. 3-7</reference>. III. He instructs and establishes them in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ to judgment, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8-2Pet.3.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. IV. He sets forth the use and improvement which Christians ought to make of Christ's second coming, and that dissolution and renovation of things which will accompany that solemn coming of our Lord, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.11-2Pet.3.18">ver. 11-18</reference>.
entries.97d6a9f66a4d5bc2327dd9f9fde998c5b1758956: <div eID="gen33592" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33591" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Adhere to Words of the Prophets and Commandments of the Apostles. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33593" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you; in <hi type="italic">both</hi> which I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance: <hi type="super">2</hi> That ye may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour: <div eID="gen33593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33594" type="x-p"/> That the apostle might the better reach his end in writing this epistle, which is to make them steady and constant in a fiducial and practical remembrance of the doctrine of the gospel, he, 1. Expresses his special affection and tenderness for them, by calling them <hi type="italic">beloved,</hi> hereby evidencing that he <hi type="italic">added to godliness brotherly-kindness,</hi> as he had (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.17">ch. i. 17</reference>) exhorted them to do. Ministers must be examples of love and affection, as well as life and conversation. 2. He evinces a sincere love to them, and hearty concern for them, by writing the same thing to them, though in other words. It being safe for them, it shall not be grievous to him to write upon the same subject, and pursue the same design, by those methods which are most likely to succeed. 3. The better to recommend the matter, he tells them that what he would have them to remember are, (1.) <hi type="italic">The words spoken by the holy prophets,</hi> who were divinely inspired, both enlightened and sanctified by the Holy Ghost; and, seeing these persons' minds were purified by the sanctifying operation of the same Spirit, they were the better disposed to receive and retain what came from God by the holy prophets. (2.) <hi type="italic">The commandments of the apostles of the Lord and Saviour;</hi> and therefore the disciples and servants of Christ ought to regard what those who are sent by him have declared unto them to be the will of their Lord. What God has spoken by the prophets of the Old Testament, and Christ has commanded by the apostles of the New, cannot but demand and deserve to be frequently remembered; and those who meditate on these things will feel the quickening virtues thereof. It is by these things the pure minds of Christians are to be stirred up, that they may be active and lively in the work of holiness, and zealous and unwearied in the way to heaven.
entries.11679f5d5b3ff9c702f0412f49dfe5d75bc191e6: <div eID="gen33594" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cavils of Infidels; Destruction of the World. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33595" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, <hi type="super">4</hi> And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as <hi type="italic">they were</hi> from the beginning of the creation. <hi type="super">5</hi> For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water: <hi type="super">6</hi> Whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished: <hi type="super">7</hi> But the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men. <div eID="gen33595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33596" type="x-p"/> To quicken and excite us to a serious minding and firm adhering to what God has revealed to us by the prophets and apostles, we are told that there will be <hi type="italic">scoffers,</hi> men who will <hi type="italic">make a mock of sin,</hi> and of salvation from it. God's way of saving sinners by Jesus Christ is what men will scoff at, and that <hi type="italic">in the last days,</hi> under the gospel. This indeed may seem very strange, that the New-Testament dispensation of the covenant of grace, which is spiritual and therefore more agreeable to the nature of God than the Old, should be ridiculed and reproached; but the spirituality and simplicity of New-Testament worship are directly contrary to the carnal mind of man, and this accounts for what the apostle seems here to hint at, namely, that scoffers shall be more numerous and more bold in the last days than ever before. Though in all ages those who were born and walked after the flesh persecuted, reviled, and reproached those who were born and did walk after the Spirit, yet in the last days there will be a great improvement in the art and impudence of bantering serious godliness, and those who firmly adhere to the circumspection and self-denial which the gospel prescribes. This is what is mentioned as a thing well known to all Christians, and therefore they ought to reckon upon it, that they may not be surprised and shaken, as if some strange thing happened unto them. Now to prevent the true Christian's being overcome, when attacked by these scoffers, we are told, <div eID="gen33596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33597" type="x-p"/> I. What sort of persons they are: they <hi type="italic">walk after their own lusts,</hi> they follow the devices and desires of their own hearts, and carnal affections, not the dictates and directions of right reason and an enlightened well-informed judgment. This they do in the course of their conversation, they live as they list, and they speak as they list; it is not only their inward minds that are evil and opposite to God, as the mind of every unrenewed sinner is (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">Rom. viii. 7</reference>), alienated from God, ignorant of him, and averse to him; but they have grown to such a height of wickedness that they proclaim openly what is in the hearts of others who are yet carnal; they say, "Our tongues are our own, and our strength, and time, and <hi type="italic">who is lord over us?</hi> Who shall contradict or control us, or ever call us to an account for what we say or do?" And, as they scorn to be confined by any laws of God in their conversation, so neither will they bear that the revelation of God should dictate and prescribe to them what they are to believe; as they will walk in their own way, and talk their own language, so will they also think their own thoughts, and form principles which are altogether their own: here also <hi type="italic">their own lusts</hi> alone shall be consulted by them. None but such accomplished libertines as are here described can take a seat, at least they cannot sit in the seat of the scornful. "By this you shall know them, that you may the better be upon your guard against them." <div eID="gen33597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33598" type="x-p"/> II. We also are forewarned how far they will proceed: they will attempt to shake and unsettle us, even as to our belief of Christ's second coming; they will scoffingly say, <hi type="italic">Where is the promise of his coming?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">v. 4</reference>. Without this, all the other articles of the Christian faith will signify very little; this is that which fills up and gives the finishing stroke to all the rest. The promised Messiah has come, he <hi type="italic">was made flesh, and dwelt among us;</hi> he is altogether such a one as in stated before, and has done all that for us which has been before taken notice of. These principles the enemies of Christianity have all along endeavoured to overturn; but as these all rest upon facts which are already past, and of which this and the other apostles have given us the most sure and satisfying evidence, it is probable that they will at last grow weary of their opposition to them; and yet, while one very principal article of our faith refers to what is still behind, and only has a promise to rest upon, here they will still attack us, even to the end of time. Till our Lord shall have come, they will not themselves believe that he will come; nay, they will laugh at the very mention of his second coming, and do what in them lies to put all out of countenance who seriously believe and wait for it. Now therefore let us see how this point stands, both on the believer's part and on the part of these seducers: the believer not only desires that he may come, but, having a promise that he will come, a promise that he himself has made and often repeated, a promise received and reported by faithful witnesses, and left upon sure record, he is also firmly and fully persuaded that he will come: on the other hand, these seducers, because they wish he never may, therefore do all that in them lies to cheat themselves and others into a persuasion that he will never come. If they cannot deny that there is a promise, yet they will laugh at that very promise, which argues much higher degrees of infidelity and contempt: <hi type="italic">Where is the promise,</hi> say they, <hi type="italic">of his coming?</hi> <div eID="gen33598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33599" type="x-p"/> III. We are also forewarned of the method of their reasoning, for while they laugh they will pretend to argue too. To this purpose they add that <hi type="italic">since the fathers fell asleep all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">v. 4</reference>. This is a subtle, though not a solid way of reasoning; it is apt to make impressions upon weak minds, and especially upon wicked hearts. <hi type="italic">Because sentence against them is not speedily executed,</hi> therefore they flatter themselves that it never will, whereupon <hi type="italic">their hearts are fully set in them to do evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Eccl. viii. 11</reference>); thus they act themselves, and thus they would persuade others to act; so here, say they, "<hi type="italic">The fathers have fallen asleep,</hi> those are all dead to whom <hi type="italic">the promise was made,</hi> and it was never made good in their time, and there is no likelihood that it ever will be in any time; why should we trouble ourselves about it? If there had been any truth or certainty in the promise you speak of, we should surely have seen somewhat of it before this time, some signs of his coming, some preparatory steps in order to it; whereas we find to this very day <hi type="italic">all things continue as they were,</hi> without any change, even <hi type="italic">from the beginning of the creation.</hi> Since the world has undergone no changes in the course of so many thousand years, why should we affright ourselves as if it were to have an end?" Thus do these scoffers argue. <hi type="italic">Because they see no changes, therefore they fear not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Ps. lv. 19</reference>. They neither fear him nor his judgments; what he never has done they would conclude he never can do or never will. <div eID="gen33599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33600" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is the falsehood of their argument detected. Whereas they confidently had said there had not been any change <hi type="italic">from the beginning of the creation,</hi> the apostle puts us in remembrance of a change already past, which, in a manner, equals that which we are called to expect and look for, which was the drowning of the world in the days of Noah. This these scoffers had overlooked; they took no notice of it. Though they might have known it, and ought to have known it, yet <hi type="italic">this they willingly are ignorant of</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5">v. 5</reference>), they choose to pass it over in silence, as if they had never heard or known any thing of it; if they knew it, they did not like to retain it in their knowledge; they did not receive this truth in the love of it, neither did they care to own it. Note, It is hard to persuade men to believe what they are not willing to find true; they are ignorant, in many cases, because they are willing to be ignorant, and they do not know because they do not care to know. But let not sinners think that such ignorance as this will be admitted as an excuse for whatever sin it may betray them into. Those who crucified Christ did not know who he was; for <hi type="italic">had they known they would not have crucified the Lord of glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>); but, though ignorant, they were not therefore innocent; their ignorance itself was a sin, willing and wilful ignorance, and one sin can be no excuse for another. So it is here; had these known of the dreadful vengeance with which God swept away a whole world of ungodly wretches at once, they would not surely have scoffed at his threatenings of any after equally terrible judgment; but here <hi type="italic">they were willingly ignorant,</hi> they did not know what God had done because they had no mind to know it. Now therefore we shall proceed to consider the representation which the apostle here lays down both of the destruction of the old world by water and that which awaits this present world at the final conflagration. He mentions the one as what God has done, to convince and persuade us the rather to believe that the other both may be and will be. <div eID="gen33600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33601" type="x-p"/> 1. We begin with the apostle's account of the destruction which has once already come upon the world (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5-2Pet.3.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">By the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water, whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished.</hi> Originally the world was otherwise situated, the waters were most wisely divided at the creation and most beneficially for us; some of the waters had proper repositories above the firmament, here called the heavens (as it is also <reference osisRef="Gen.1.8">Gen. i. 8</reference>), and others, under the firmament, gathered together unto one place; there were then both sea and dry land, commodious habitation for the children of men. But now, at the time of the universal deluge, the case is strangely altered; the waters which God had divided before, assigning to each part its convenient receptacle, now does he, in anger, throw together again in a heap. <hi type="italic">He breaks up the fountain of the great deep, and throws open the windows (that is, the clouds) of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen. vii. 11</reference>), till the whole earth is overflowed with water, and not a spot can be found upon the highest mountains but what is <hi type="italic">fifteen cubits under water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.7.20">Gen. vii. 20</reference>. Thus he made known at once his terrible power and his fierce anger, and made an end of a whole world at once: <hi type="italic">The world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Is not here a change and a most awful change! And then it is to be observed that all this was done by the word of God; it was by his powerful word that the world was made at first, and made in so commodious and beautiful a frame and order, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.3">Heb. xi. 3</reference>, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Katertisthai</hi></hi>. <hi type="italic">He said, Let there be a firmament,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Gen.1.6-Gen.1.7">Gen. i. 6, 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">And let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9-2Pet.3.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Thus he spoke, and it was done, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.9">Ps. xxxiii. 9</reference>. Thus, says our apostle, <hi type="italic">by the word of the Lord the heavens were,</hi> as they were <hi type="italic">of old</hi> (that is, at first creation) <hi type="italic">and the earth</hi> (as it was at first a terraqueous globe) <hi type="italic">standing out of the water and in the water.</hi> Not is it only the first frame and order of the world that is here said to be <hi type="italic">by the word of God,</hi> but the after-confusion and ruin of the world, as well as the utter destruction of its inhabitants, were also by the same word; none but that God who <hi type="italic">stretched out the heavens and laid the foundation of the earth</hi> could destroy and overthrow such a vast fabric at once. This was done by the word of his power, and it was also done according to the word of his promise; God had said that he would destroy man, even all flesh, and that he would do it by bringing a flood of waters upon the earth, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.7">Gen. vi. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.17">17</reference>. This was the change which God had before brought upon the world, and which these scoffers had overlooked; and now we are to consider, <div eID="gen33601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33602" type="x-p"/> 2. What the apostle says of the destructive change which is yet to come upon it: <hi type="italic">The heavens and the earth, which now are, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.7">v. 7</reference>. Here we have an awful account of the final dissolution of the world, and which we are yet more nearly concerned in. The ruin that came upon the world and its inhabitants by the flood, we read, and hear, and think of, with concern, though those who were swept away by it were such as we never knew; but the judgment here spoken of is yet to come, and will surely come, though we know not when, nor upon what particular age or generation of men; and therefore we are not, we cannot be, sure that it may not happen in our own times: and this makes a very great difference, though it should be admitted that they were equal in every other respect, which yet must not be allowed, for there were some, though very few, who escaped that deluge, but not one can escape in this conflagration. Besides, we were not in reach of the one, but are not sure that we shall not be included in the other calamity. Now therefore to see the world to which we belong destroyed at once—not a single person only, not a particular family only, nor yet a nation (even that which we are most nearly interested in and concerned for), but the whole world, I say, sinking at once, and no ark provided, no possible way left of escaping for any one from the common ruin, this makes a difference between the desolation that has been and what we yet are to expect. The one is already past, and never to return upon us any more (for God has said expressly <hi type="italic">that there shall never any more be a flood to destroy the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.9.11-Gen.9.17">Gen. ix. 11-17</reference>); the other is still behind, and is as certain to come as the truth and the power of God can make it: the one came gradually upon the world, and was growing upon its inhabitants forty days, before it made an utter end of them (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.12">Gen. vii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.17">17</reference>); this other will come upon them swiftly and all at once (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.1">2 Pet. ii. 1</reference>): besides, there were in that overthrow (as we have said) a few who escaped, but the ruin which yet awaits this world, whenever it comes, will be absolutely a universal one; there will not be any part but what the devouring flames will seize upon, not a sanctuary left any where for the inhabitants to flee to, not a single spot in all this world where any one of them can be safe. Thus, whatever differences may be assigned between that destruction of the world and this here spoken of, they do indeed represent the approaching as the most terrible judgment; yet that the world has once been destroyed by a universal deluge renders it the more credible that it may be again ruined by a universal conflagration. Let therefore the scoffers, who laugh at the coming of our Lord to judgment, at least consider that it <hi type="italic">may be.</hi> There is nothing said of it in the word of God but what is within reach of the power of God, and, though they still should laugh, they shall not put us out of countenance; we are well assured that it will be, because he has said it, and we can depend upon his <hi type="italic">promise.</hi> They <hi type="italic">err, not knowing</hi> (at least not believing) <hi type="italic">the scriptures, nor the power of God;</hi> but we know, and we do or ought to depend upon, both. Now that which he has said, and which he will certainly make good, is that <hi type="italic">the heavens and the earth which now are</hi> (which we are now related to, which still subsist in all the beauty and order in which we see them, and which are so agreeable and useful to us, as we find they are) <hi type="italic">are kept in store,</hi> not to be, what earthly minds would wish to have them, treasures for us, but to be what God will have them, in his treasury, securely lodged and kept safely for his purposes. It follows, they are <hi type="italic">reserved unto fire.</hi> Observe, God's following judgments are more terrible than those which went before; the old world was destroyed by water, but this is reserved unto fire, which shall burn up the wicked at the last day; and, though this seems to be delayed, yet, as this wicked world is upheld by the word of God, so it is only reserved for the vengeance of him to whom vengeance belongs, who will at the day of judgment deal with an ungodly world according to their deserts, for the day of judgment is the day of <hi type="italic">the perdition of ungodly men.</hi> Those who now scoff at a future judgment shall find it a day of vengeance and utter destruction. "Beware therefore of being among these scoffers; never question but the day of the Lord will come; give diligence therefore to be found in Christ, that that may be a time of refreshment and day of redemption to you which will be a day of indignation and wrath to the ungodly world."
entries.867f0eb154e6b910757210cab439531900dd83b5: <div eID="gen33602" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conception of Eternity. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33603" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day <hi type="italic">is</hi> with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. <div eID="gen33603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33604" type="x-p"/> The apostle comes in these words to instruct and establish Christians in the truth of the coming of the Lord, where we may clearly discern the tenderness and affection wherewith he speaks to them, calling them <hi type="italic">beloved;</hi> he had a compassionate concern and a love of good-will for the ungodly wretches who refused to believe divine revelation, but he has a peculiar respect for the true believers, and the remaining ignorance and weakness that the apprehends to be in them make him jealous, and put him on giving them a caution. Here we may observe, <div eID="gen33604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33605" type="x-p"/> I. The truth which the apostle asserts—<hi type="italic">that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years are as one day.</hi> Though, in the account of men, there is a great deal of difference between a day and a year, and a vast deal more between one day and a thousand years, yet in the account of God, who inhabits eternity, in which there is no succession, there is no difference; for all things past, present, and future, are ever before him, and the delay of a thousand years cannot be so much to him as the deferring of any thing for a day or an hour is to us. <div eID="gen33605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33606" type="x-p"/> II. The importance of this truth: This is the <hi type="italic">one thing</hi> the apostle would not have us ignorant of; a holy awe and reverential fear of God are necessary in order to our worshiping and glorifying him, and a belief of the inconceivable distance between him and us is very proper to beget and maintain that religious fear of the Lord which is the beginning of wisdom. This is a truth that belongs to our peace, and therefore he endeavours that it may not be hidden from our eyes; as it is in the original, <hi type="italic">Let not this one thing be hidden from you.</hi> If men have no knowledge or belief of the eternal God, they will be very apt to think him such a one as themselves. Yet how hard is it to conceive of eternity! It is therefore not very easy to attain such a knowledge of God as is absolutely necessary.
entries.f464c724f7581963156caea91907c085c4b9126b: <div eID="gen33606" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Destruction of the World. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33607" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. <hi type="super">10</hi> But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up. <div eID="gen33607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33608" type="x-p"/> We are here told that <hi type="italic">the Lord is not slack</hi>—he does not delay beyond the appointed time; as God kept the time that he had appointed for the delivering of Israel out of Egypt, to a day (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exod. xii. 41</reference>), so he will keep to the time appointed in coming to judge the world. What a difference is there between the account which God makes and that which men make! Good men are apt to think God stays beyond the appointed time, that is, the time which they have set for their own and the church's deliverance; but they set one time and God sets another, and he will not fail to keep the day which he has appointed. Ungodly men dare charge a culpable slackness upon God, as if he had slipped the time, and laid aside the thoughts of coming. But the apostle assures us, <div eID="gen33608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33609" type="x-p"/> I. That what men count slackness is truly <hi type="italic">long-suffering,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">to us-ward;</hi> it is giving more time to his own people, <hi type="italic">whom he has chosen before the foundation of the world,</hi> many of whom are not as yet converted; and those who are in a state of grace and favour with God are to advance in knowledge and holiness, and in the exercise of faith and patience, to abound in good works, doing and suffering what they are called to, that they may bring glory to God, and improve in a meetness for heaven; for God is not willing that any of these should perish, but that all of them should come to repentance. Here observe, 1. Repentance is absolutely necessary in order to salvation. <hi type="italic">Except we repent, we shall perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.13.3">Luke xiii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.5">5</reference>. 2. God has no delight in the death of sinners: as the punishment of sinners is a torment to his creatures, a merciful God does not take pleasure in it; and though the principal design of God in his long-suffering is the blessedness of those <hi type="italic">whom he has chosen to salvation, through sanctification of the spirit, and belief of the truth,</hi> yet his goodness and forbearance do in their own nature invite and call to repentance all those to whom they are exercised; and, if men continue impenitent when God gives them space to repent, he will deal more severely with them, though the great reason why he did not hasten his coming was because he had not accomplished <hi type="italic">the number of his elect.</hi> "Abuse not therefore the patience and long-suffering of God, by abandoning yourselves to a course of ungodliness; presume not to go on boldly in the way of sinners, nor to sit down securely in an unconverted impenitent state, as he who said (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.48">Matt. xxiv. 48</reference>), <hi type="italic">My Lord delayeth his coming,</hi> lest he come and surprise you;" for, <div eID="gen33609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33610" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">v. 10</reference>. Here we may observe, 1. The certainty of the day of the Lord: though it is now above sixteen hundred years since this epistle was written, and the day has not yet come, it assuredly will come. God has <hi type="italic">appointed a day wherein he will judge the world in righteousness,</hi> and he will keep his appointment. <hi type="italic">It is appointed to men once to die, and after this the judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.27">Heb. ix. 27</reference>. "Settle it therefore in your hearts that the day of the Lord will certainly come, and you shall certainly be called to give an account of all things done in the body, whether good or evil; and let your exact walking before God, and your frequent judging yourselves, evidence your firm belief of a future judgment, when many live as if they were never to give any account at all." 2. The suddenness of this day: It <hi type="italic">will come as a thief in the night,</hi> at a time when men are sleeping and secure, and have no manner of apprehension or expectation of the day of the Lord, any more than men have of a thief when they are in a deep sleep, in the dark and silent night. <hi type="italic">At midnight there was a cry, Behold, the bridegroom comes,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">Matt. xxv. 6</reference>), and at that time not only the foolish, but also the wise virgins slumbered and slept. <hi type="italic">The Lord will come in a day when we look not for him, and an hour when men are not aware.</hi> The time which men think to be the most improper and unlikely, and when therefore they are most secure, will be the time of the Lord's coming. Let us then beware how we in our thoughts and imaginations put that day far away from us; but rather suppose it to be so much nearer in reality, by how much further off it is in the opinion of the ungodly world. 3. The solemnity of this coming. (1.) <hi type="italic">The heavens shall pass away with a great noise.</hi> The visible heavens, as unable to abide when the Lord shall come in his glory, shall pass away; they shall undergo a mighty alteration, and this shall be very sudden, and with such a noise as the breaking and tumbling down of so great a fabric must necessarily occasion. (2.) <hi type="italic">The elements shall melt with fervent heat.</hi> At this coming of the Lord it shall not only be very <hi type="italic">tempestuous round about him,</hi> so that the very heavens shall pass away as in a mighty violent storm, but <hi type="italic">a fire shall go before him, that shall melt the elements</hi> of which the creatures are composed. (3.) <hi type="italic">The earth also, and all the works that are therein, shall be burnt up.</hi> The earth, and its inhabitants, and all the works that are therein, shall be burnt up. The earth, and its inhabitants, and all the works, whether of nature or art, shall be destroyed. The stately palaces and gardens, and all the desirable things wherein worldly-minded men seek and place their happiness, all of them shall be burnt up; all sorts of creatures which God has made, and all the works of men, must submit, all must pass through the fire, which shall be a consuming fire to all that sin has brought into the world, though it may be a refining fire to the works of God's hand, that the glass of the creation being made much brighter the saints may much better discern the glory of the Lord therein. <div eID="gen33610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33611" type="x-p"/> And now who can but observe what a difference there will be between the first coming of Christ and the second! Yet that is called <hi type="italic">the great and dreadful day of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.5">Mal. iv. 5</reference>. How much more dreadful must this coming to judgment be! May we be so wise as to prepare for it, that it may not be a day of vengeance and destruction unto us. O! what will become of us, if we set our affections on this earth, and make it our portion, seeing all these things shall be burnt up? Look out therefore, and make sure of a happiness beyond this visible world, which must all be melted down.
entries.c08819c8e8aa86a1af189737aa7cad5dce29642d: <div eID="gen33611" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Solemn Exhortations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 67.)</title> <div sID="gen33612" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">Seeing</hi> then <hi type="italic">that</hi> all these things shall be dissolved, what manner <hi type="italic">of persons</hi> ought ye to be in <hi type="italic">all</hi> holy conversation and godliness, <hi type="super">12</hi> Looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God, wherein the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat? <hi type="super">13</hi> Nevertheless we, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness. <hi type="super">14</hi> Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless. <hi type="super">15</hi> And account <hi type="italic">that</hi> the longsuffering of our Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you; <hi type="super">16</hi> As also in all <hi type="italic">his</hi> epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as <hi type="italic">they do</hi> also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction. <hi type="super">17</hi> Ye therefore, beloved, seeing ye know <hi type="italic">these things</hi> before, beware lest ye also, being led away with the error of the wicked, fall from your own stedfastness. 18 But grow in grace, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him <hi type="italic">be</hi> glory both now and for ever. Amen. <div eID="gen33612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33613" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having instructed them in the doctrine of Christ's second coming, <div eID="gen33613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33614" type="x-p"/> I. Takes occasion thence to exhort them to purity and godliness in their whole conversation: all the truths which are revealed in scripture should be improved for our advancement in practical godliness: this is the effect that knowledge must produce, or we are never the better for it. <hi type="italic">If you know these things, happy are you if you do them. Seeing all these things must be dissolved, how holy should we be,</hi> that are assured of it, departing from and dying to sin, that has so corrupted and defiled all the visible creation that there is an absolute need of its dissolution! All that was made for man's use is subject to vanity by man's sin: and if the sin of man has brought the visible heavens, and the elements and earth, under a curse, from which they cannot be freed without being dissolved, what an abominable evil is sin, and how much to be hated by us! And, inasmuch as this dissolution is in order to their being restored to their primitive beauty and excellency, how pure and holy should we be, in order to our being fit for the <hi type="italic">new heaven and new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness!</hi> It is a very exact and universal holiness that he exhorts to, not resting in any lower measure or degree, but labouring to be eminent beyond what is commonly attained—holy in God's house and in our own, holy in our worshipping of God and in our conversing with men. All our conversation, whether with high or low, rich or poor, good or bad, friends or enemies, must be holy. We must <hi type="italic">keep ourselves unspotted from the world</hi> in all our converses with it. We must be <hi type="italic">perfecting holiness in the fear of God,</hi> and in the love of God too. We must <hi type="italic">exercise ourselves unto godliness</hi> of all sorts, in all its parts, trusting in God and delighting in God only, who continues the same when the whole visible creation shall be dissolved, devoting ourselves to the service of God, and designing the glorifying and enjoyment of God, who endures for ever; whereas what worldly men delight in and follow after must all be dissolved. Those things which we now see must in a little while pass away, and be no more as they now are: let us look therefore at what shall abide and continue, which, though it be not present, is certain and not far off. This <hi type="italic">looking for the day of God</hi> is one of the directions the apostle gives us, in order to our being eminently <hi type="italic">holy and godly in all manner of conversation.</hi> "Look for the day of God as what you firmly believe shall come, and what you earnestly long for." <hi type="italic">The coming of the day of God</hi> is what every Christian must hope for and earnestly expect; for it is a day when Christ shall <hi type="italic">appear in the glory of the Father,</hi> and evidence his divinity and Godhead even to those who counted him a mere man. The first coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, when he <hi type="italic">appeared in the form of a servant,</hi> was what the people of God earnestly waited and looked for: that coming was for <hi type="italic">the consolation of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.25">Luke ii. 25</reference>. How much more should they wait with expectation and earnestness for his second coming, which will be the day of their complete redemption, and of his most glorious manifestation! Then he shall <hi type="italic">come to be admired in his saints, and glorified in all those that believe.</hi> For though it cannot but terrify and affright the ungodly to see the visible heavens all in a flame, and the elements melting, yet the believer, whose <hi type="italic">faith is the evidence of things not seen,</hi> can rejoice in hope of more glorious heavens after these have been melted and refined by that dreadful fire which shall burn up all the dross of this visible creation. Here we must take notice, 1. What true Christians look for: <hi type="italic">new heavens and a new earth,</hi> in which a great deal more of the wisdom, power and goodness of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ will be clearly discerned than we are able to discover in what we now see; for in these new heavens and earth, freed from the vanity the former were subject to, and the sin they were polluted with, only righteousness shall dwell; this is to be the habitation of such righteous persons as do righteousness, and are free from the power and pollution of sin; <hi type="italic">all the wicked shall be turned into hell;</hi> those only who are clothed with a righteousness of Christ, and sanctified by the Holy Ghost, shall be admitted to dwell in this holy place. 2. What is the ground and foundation of this expectation and hope—<hi type="italic">the promise of God.</hi> To look for any thing which God has not promised is presumption; but if our expectations are according to the promise, both as to the things we look for and the time and way of their being brought about, we cannot meet with a disappointment; <hi type="italic">for he is faithful who has promised.</hi> "See therefore that you raise and regulate your expectations of all the great things that are to come according to the word of God; and, as to <hi type="italic">the new heaven and new earth,</hi> look for them as God has allowed and directed by the passages we have in this portion of scripture how before you, and in <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa. lxv. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.22">lxvi. 22</reference>, to which the apostle may be thought to allude." <div eID="gen33614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33615" type="x-p"/> II. As in <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.11">v. 11</reference> he exhorts to holiness from the consideration that <hi type="italic">the heavens and the earth shall be dissolved,</hi> so in <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">v. 14</reference> he resumes his exhortation from the consideration that they shall be again renewed. "Seeing you expect the day of God, when our Lord Jesus Christ will appear in his glorious majesty, and these heavens and earth shall be dissolved and melted down, and, being purified and refined, shall be erected and rebuilt, prepare to meet him. It nearly concerns you to see in what state you will be when the Judge of all the world shall come to pass sentence upon men, and to determine how it shall be with them to all eternity. This is the court of judicature whence there lies no appeal; whatever sentence is here passed by this great Judge is irreversible; therefore get ready to <hi type="italic">appear before the judgment-seat of Christ:</hi> and see to it," <div eID="gen33615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33616" type="x-p"/> 1. "That you be <hi type="italic">found of him in peace,</hi> in a state of peace and reconciliation with God through Christ, in whom alone God is <hi type="italic">reconciling the world to himself.</hi> All that are out of Christ are in a state of enmity, and reject and oppose the Lord and his anointed, and shall therefore <hi type="italic">be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and the glory of his power.</hi> Those whose sins are pardoned and their peace made with God are the only safe and happy people; therefore follow after peace, and that with all." (1.) Peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. (2.) Peace in our own consciences, through the Spirit of grace witnessing with our spirits that we are the children of God. (3.) Peace with men, by having a calm and peaceable disposition wrought in us, resembling that of our blessed Lord. <div eID="gen33616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33617" type="x-p"/> 2. That you be <hi type="italic">found of Christ without spot, and blameless. Follow after holiness</hi> as well as peace: and even spotless and perfect; we must not only take heed of all spots which are not the spots of God's children (this only prevents our being found of men without spot), we must be pressing towards spotless purity, absolute perfection. Christians must be <hi type="italic">perfecting holiness,</hi> that they may be not only blameless before men, but also in the sight of God; and all this deserves and needs the greatest diligence; he who does this work negligently can never do it successfully. "Never expect to be found at that day of God in peace, if you are lazy and idle in this your day, in which we must finish the work that is given us to do. It is only the diligent Christian who will be the happy Christian in the day of the Lord. Our Lord will suddenly come to us, or shortly call us to him; and would you have him find you idle?" Remember there is a curse denounced against him <hi type="italic">who does the work of the Lord negligently,</hi> Marg. <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jer. xlviii. 10</reference>. Heaven will be a sufficient recompence for all our diligence and industry; therefore let us labour and take pains in the work of the Lord; he will certainly reward us if we be diligent in the work he has allotted us; now, that you may be diligent, <hi type="italic">account the long-suffering of our Lord to be salvation.</hi> "Does your Lord delay his coming? Do not think this is to give more time to make provision for your lusts, to gratify them; it is so much space to repent and work out your salvation. It proceeds not from a want of concern or compassion for his suffering servants, nor is it designed to give countenance and encouragement to the world of the ungodly, but that men may have time to prepare for eternity. Learn then to make a right use of the patience of our Lord, who does as yet delay his coming. Follow after peace and holiness, or else his coming will be dreadful to you." And inasmuch as it is difficult to prevent men's abuse of God's patience, and engage them in the right improvement thereof, our apostle quotes St. Paul as directing men to make the same good use of the divine forbearance, that in the mouth, or from the pen, of two apostles the truth might be confirmed. And we may here observe with what esteem and affection he speaks of him who had formerly publicly withstood and sharply reproved Peter. If a righteous man smite one who is truly religious, it shall be received as a kindness; and let him reprove, it shall be as an excellent oil, which shall soften and sweeten the good man that is reproved when he does amiss. What an honourable mention does this apostle of the circumcision make of that very man who had openly, <hi type="italic">before all, reproved him,</hi> as not walking uprightly according to the truth of the gospel! (1.) He calls him <hi type="italic">brother,</hi> whereby he means not only that he is a fellow-christian (in which sense the word brethren is used <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.27">1 Thess. v. 27</reference>), or a fellow-preacher (in which sense Paul calls Timothy the evangelist a <hi type="italic">brother,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.1">Col. i. 1</reference>), but a fellow-apostle, one who had the same extraordinary commission, immediately from Christ himself, to preach the gospel in every place, and to disciple all nations. Though many seducing teachers denied Paul's apostleship, yet Peter owns him to be an apostle. (2.) He calls him <hi type="italic">beloved;</hi> and they being both alike commissioned, and both united in the same service of the same Lord, it would have been very unseemly if they had not been united in affection to one another, for the strengthening of one another's hands, mutually desirous of, and rejoicing in, one another's success. (3.) He mentions Paul as one who had an uncommon measure of wisdom given unto him. He was a person of eminent knowledge in the mysteries of the gospel, and did neither in that nor any other qualification come behind any of all the other apostles. How desirable is it that those who preach the same gospel should treat one another according to the pattern Peter here sets them! It is surely their duty to endeavour, by proper methods, to prevent or remove all prejudices that hinder ministers' usefulness, and to beget and improve the esteem and respect in the minds of people towards their ministers that may promote the success of their labours. And let us also here observe, [1.] The excellent wisdom that was in Paul is said to be <hi type="italic">given</hi> him. The understanding and knowledge that qualify men to preach the gospel are the gift of God. We must seek for knowledge, and labour to get understanding, in hopes that it shall be given us from above, while we are diligent in using proper means to attain it. [2.] The apostle imparts to men according as he had received from God. He endeavours to lead others as far as he himself was led into the knowledge of the mysteries of the gospel. He is not an intruder into the things he had not seen or been fully assured of, and yet he does not fail to declare the whole counsel of God, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Acts xx. 27</reference>. [3.] The epistles which were written by the apostle of the Gentiles, and directed to those Gentiles who believed in Christ, are designed for the instruction and edification of those who from among the Jews were brought to believe in Christ; for it is generally thought that what is here alluded to is contained in the epistle to the Romans (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">ch. ii. 4</reference>), though in all his epistles there are some things that refer to one or other of the subjects treated of in this and the foregoing chapter; and it cannot seem strange that those who were pursuing the same general design should in their epistles insist upon the same things. But the apostle Peter proceeds to tell us that in those things which are to be met with in Paul's epistles there are some things hard to be understood. Among the variety of subjects treated of in scripture, some are not easy to be understood because of their own obscurity, such are prophecies; others cannot be so easily understood because of their excellency and sublimity, as the mysterious doctrines; and others are with difficulty taken in because of the weakness of men's minds, such are the things of the Spirit of God, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. And here the unlearned and unstable make wretched work; for they wrest and torture the scriptures, to make them speak what the Holy Ghost did not intend. Those who are not well instructed and well established in the truth are in great danger of perverting the word of God. Those who have heard and learned of the Father are best secured from misunderstanding and misapplying any part of the word of God; and, where there is a divine power to establish as well as to instruct men in divine truth, persons are effectually secured from falling into errors. How great a blessing this is we learn by observing what is the pernicious consequence of the errors that ignorant and unstable men fall into—even their own destruction. Errors in particular concerning the holiness and justice of God are the utter ruin of multitudes of men. Let us therefore earnestly pray for the Spirit of God to instruct us in the truth, that we may know it as it is in Jesus, and have our hearts established with grace, that we may stand firm and unshaken, even in the most stormy times, when others are tossed to and fro with every wind of doctrine. <div eID="gen33617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33618" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle gives them a word of caution, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.17-2Pet.3.18">v. 17, 18</reference>, where, <div eID="gen33618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33619" type="x-p"/> 1. He intimates that the knowledge we have of these things should make us very wary and watchful, inasmuch as there is a twofold danger, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.17">v. 17</reference>. (1.) We are in great danger <hi type="italic">of</hi> being seduced, and turned away from the truth. The unlearned and unstable, and they are very numerous, do generally wrest the scripture. Many who have the scriptures and read them do not understand what they read; and too many of those who have a right understanding of the sense and meaning of the word are not established in the belief of the truth, and all these are liable to fall into error. Few attain to the knowledge and acknowledgment of doctrinal Christianity; and fewer find, so as to keep in the way of practical godliness, which is the narrow way, which only leadeth unto life. There must be a great deal of self-denial and suspicion of ourselves, and submitting to the authority of Christ Jesus our great prophet, before we can heartily receive all the truths of the gospel, and therefore we are in great danger of rejecting the truth. (2.) We are in great danger <hi type="italic">by</hi> being seduced; for, [1.] So far as we are turned from the truth <hi type="italic">so far are we turned out of the way to true blessedness,</hi> into the path which leads to destruction. If men corrupt the word of God, it tends to their own utter ruin. [2.] When men wrest the word of God, <hi type="italic">they fall into the error of the wicked,</hi> men without law, who keep to no rules, set no bounds to themselves, a sort of free-thinkers, which the psalmist detests. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.113">Ps. cxix. 113</reference>, <hi type="italic">I hate vain thoughts, but thy law do I love.</hi> Whatever opinions and thoughts of men are not conformable to the law of God, and warranted by it, the good man disclaims and abhors; they are the conceits and counsels of the ungodly, who have forsaken God's law, and, if we imbibe their opinions, we shall too soon imitate their practices. [3.] Those who are led away by error <hi type="italic">fall from their own stedfastness.</hi> They are wholly unhinged and unsettled, and know not where to rest, but are at the greatest uncertainty, like a wave of the sea, driven with the wind and tossed. It nearly concerns us therefore to be upon our guard, seeing the danger is so great. <div eID="gen33619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33620" type="x-p"/> 2. That we may the better avoid being led away, the apostle directs us what to do, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.18">v. 18</reference>. And, (1.) We must <hi type="italic">grow in grace.</hi> He had in the beginning of the epistle exhorted us to add one grace to another, and here he advises us to grow in all grace, in faith, and virtue, and knowledge. By how much the stronger grace is in us, by so much the more stedfast shall we be in the truth. (2.) We must grow <hi type="italic">in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> "Follow on to know the Lord. Labour to know him more clearly and more fully, to know more of Christ and to know him to better purpose, so as to be more like him and to love him better." This is the knowledge of Christ the apostle Paul reached after and desired to attain, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.10">Phil. iii. 10</reference>. Such a knowledge of Christ as conforms us more to him, and endears him more to us, must needs be of great use to us, to preserve us from falling off in times of general apostasy; and those who experience this effect of the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ will, upon receiving such grace from him, give thanks and praise to him, and join with our apostle in saying, <hi type="italic">To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.</hi>  <chapter eID="2Pet.3"/> <div eID="gen33620" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen33537" osisID="2Pet" type="book"/>

entries.3743d55fd14866a407e1e8285e564744f7c763bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18875"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen40454" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.1-2Pet.3.18">2Pe 3:1-18</reference>. Sureness of Christ's Coming, and Its Accompaniments, Declared in Opposition to Scoffers about to Arise. God's Long Suffering a Motive to Repentance, as Paul's Epistles Set Forth; Concluding Exhortation to Growth in the Knowledge of Christ.<div eID="gen40454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18875"/><hi type="bold">1. now--</hi>"This now a second Epistle I write." Therefore he had lately written the former Epistle. The seven Catholic Epistles were written by James, John, and Jude, shortly before their deaths; previously, while having the prospect of being still for some time alive, they felt it less necessary to write [Bengel].<div eID="gen40455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto you--</hi>The Second Epistle, though more general in its address, yet included especially the same persons as the First Epistle was particularly addressed to.<div eID="gen40456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pure--</hi>literally, "pure when examined by sunlight"; "sincere." Adulterated with no error. Opposite to "having the understanding darkened." Alford explains, The mind, will, and affection, in relation to the outer world, being turned to God [the Sun of the soul], and not obscured by fleshly and selfish regards.<div eID="gen40457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by way of--</hi>Greek, "in," "in putting you in remembrance" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.12">2Pe 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>). Ye already know (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3">2Pe 3:3</reference>); it is only needed that I remind you (Jude 5). <div eID="gen40458" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbfa8024527a81d56098a4a3f43dc4e188867ea9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18876"/><div sID="gen40459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18876"/><hi type="bold">2. prophets--</hi>of the Old Testament.<div eID="gen40459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of us--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and Vulgate read, "And of the commandment of the Lord and Saviour (declared) by YOUR apostles" (so "apostle of the Gentiles," <reference osisRef="Rom.11.13">Ro 11:13</reference>)--the apostles who live among you in the present time, in contrast to the Old Testament "prophets." <div eID="gen40460" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e52022a0712af51a627c590c30a27981735a409: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18877"/><div sID="gen40461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18877"/><hi type="bold">3. Knowing this first--</hi>from the word of the apostles.<div eID="gen40461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall come--</hi>Their very scoffing shall confirm the truth of the prediction.<div eID="gen40462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scoffers--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and Vulgate add, "(scoffers) in (that is, 'with') scoffing." As <reference osisRef="Rev.14.2">Re 14:2</reference>, "harping with harps."<div eID="gen40463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walking after their own lusts--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.10">2Pe 2:10</reference>; Jude 16, 18). Their own pleasure is their sole law, unrestrained by reverence for God. <div eID="gen40464" type="x-p"/>
entries.cba6c0b83c83d0b8f1840137e9a2f3cf005c1d07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18878"/><div sID="gen40465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18878"/>4. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.11">73:11</reference>.) Presumptuous skepticism and lawless lust, setting nature and its so-called laws above the God of nature and revelation, and arguing from the past continuity of nature's phenomena that there can be no future interruption to them, was the sin of the antediluvians, and shall be that of the scoffers in the last days.<div eID="gen40465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Where--</hi>implying that it ought to have taken place before this, if ever it was to take place, but that it never will.<div eID="gen40466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the promise--</hi>which you, believers, are so continually looking for the fulfilment of (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.13">2Pe 3:13</reference>). What becomes of the promise which you talk so much of?<div eID="gen40467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his--</hi>Christ's; the subject of prophecy from the earliest days.<div eID="gen40468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the fathers--</hi>to whom the promise was made, and who rested all their hopes on it.<div eID="gen40469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40470" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things--</hi>in the natural world; skeptics look not beyond this.<div eID="gen40470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as they were--</hi>continue as they do; as we see them to continue. From the time of the promise of Christ's coming as Saviour and King being given to the fathers, down to the present time, all things continue, and have continued, as they now are, from "the beginning of creation." The "scoffers" here are not necessarily atheists, nor do they maintain that the world existed from eternity. They are willing to recognize a God, but not the God of revelation. They reason from seeming delay against the fulfilment of God's word at all. <div eID="gen40471" type="x-p"/>
entries.5007805725c24a9215ff2af4a6ee8f8648bde7d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18879"/><div sID="gen40472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18879"/>5. Refutation of their scoffing from Scripture history.<div eID="gen40472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">willingly--</hi>wilfully; they do not wish to know. Their ignorance is voluntary.<div eID="gen40473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they ... are ignorant of--</hi>in contrast to <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8">2Pe 3:8</reference>, "Be not ignorant of this." Literally, in both verses, "This escapes THEIR notice (sagacious philosophers though they think themselves)"; "let this not escape YOUR notice." They obstinately shut their eyes to the Scripture record of the creation and the deluge; the latter is the very parallel to the coming judgment by fire, which Jesus mentions, as Peter doubtless remembered.<div eID="gen40474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the word of God--</hi>not by a fortuitous concurrence of atoms [Alford].<div eID="gen40475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of old--</hi>Greek, "from of old"; from the first beginning of all things. A confutation of their objection, "all things continue as they were FROM THE BEGINNING OF CREATION." Before the flood, the same objection to the possibility of the flood might have been urged with the same plausibility: The heavens (sky) and earth have been FROM OF OLD, how unlikely then that they should not continue so! But, replies Peter, the flood came in spite of their reasonings; so will the conflagration of the earth come in spite of the "scoffers" of the last days, changing the whole order of things (the present "world," or as Greek means, "order"), and introducing the new heavens and earth (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.13">2Pe 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen40476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth standing out of--</hi>Greek, "consisting of," that is, "formed out of the water." The waters under the firmament were at creation gathered together into one place, and the dry land emerged out of and above, them.<div eID="gen40477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in, &c.--</hi>rather, "by means of the water," as a great instrument (along with fire) in the changes wrought on the earth's surface to prepare it for man. Held together BY the water. The earth arose out of the water by the efficacy of the water itself [Tittmann]. <div eID="gen40478" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a0fe9e8ae04327c88054a8043d5bdf19618ec17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18880"/><div sID="gen40479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18880"/><hi type="bold">6. Whereby--</hi>Greek, "By which" (plural). By means of which heavens and earth (in respect to the WATERS which flowed together from both) the then world perished (that is, in respect to its occupants, men and animals, and its then existing order: not was annihilated); for in the flood "the fountains of the great deep were broken up" from the earth (1) below, and "the windows of heaven" (2) above "were opened." The earth was deluged by that water out of which it had originally risen. <div eID="gen40479" type="x-p"/>
entries.607e9c0855ccb00a0131291af15a41fb3432a184: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18881"/><div sID="gen40480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18881"/>7. (Compare <reference osisRef="Job.28.5">Job 28:5</reference>, end).<div eID="gen40480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which are now--</hi>"the postdiluvian visible world." In contrast to "that then was," <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.6">2Pe 3:6</reference>.<div eID="gen40481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same--</hi>Other oldest manuscripts read, "His" (God's).<div eID="gen40482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kept in store--</hi>Greek, "treasured up."<div eID="gen40483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reserved--</hi>"kept." It is only God's constantly watchful providence which holds together the present state of things till His time for ending it. <div eID="gen40484" type="x-p"/>
entries.96015d3e2f4b29f732f0275f45af18a675e7de59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18882"/><div sID="gen40485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18882"/><hi type="bold">8. be not ignorant--</hi>as those scoffers are (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5">2Pe 3:5</reference>). Besides the refutation of them (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5-2Pet.3.7">2Pe 3:5-7</reference>) drawn from the history of the deluge, here he adds another (addressed more to believers than to the mockers): God's delay in fulfilling His promise is not, like men's delays, owing to inability or fickleness in keeping His word, but through "long-suffering."<div eID="gen40485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this one thing--</hi>as the consideration of chief importance (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.42">Lu 10:42</reference>).<div eID="gen40486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one day ... thousand years--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.90.4">Psa 90:4</reference>): Moses there says, Thy eternity, knowing no distinction between a thousand years and a day, is the refuge of us creatures of a day. Peter views God's eternity in relation to the last day: that day seems to us, short-lived beings, long in coming, but with the Lord the interval is irrespective of the idea of long or short. His eternity exceeds all measures of time: to His divine knowledge all future things are present: His power requires not long delays for the performance of His work: His long-suffering excludes all impatient expectation and eager haste, such as we men feel. He is equally blessed in one day and in a thousand years. He can do the work of a thousand years in one day: so in <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">2Pe 3:9</reference> it is said, "He is not slack," that is, "slow": He has always the power to fulfil His "promise."<div eID="gen40487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thousand years as one day--</hi>No delay which occurs is long to God: as to a man of countless riches, a thousand guineas are as a single penny. God's oeonologe (eternal-ages measurer) differs wholly from man's horologe (hour-glass). His gnomon (dial-pointer) shows all the hours at once in the greatest activity and in perfect repose. To Him the hours pass away, neither more slowly, nor more quickly, than befits His economy. There is nothing to make Him need either to hasten or delay the end. The words, "with the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.4">Psa 90:4</reference>, "In Thy sight"), silence all man's objections on the ground of his incapability of understanding this [Bengel]. <div eID="gen40488" type="x-p"/>
entries.951e484e0230edbca3eb114c6f8f244ba7711f5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18883"/><div sID="gen40489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18883"/><hi type="bold">9. slack--</hi>slow, tardy, late; exceeding the due time, as though that time were already come. <reference osisRef="Heb.10.37">He 10:37</reference>, "will not tarry."<div eID="gen40489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his promise--</hi>which the scoffers cavil at. <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2Pe 3:4</reference>, "Where is the promise?" It shall be surely fulfilled "according to His promise" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.13">2Pe 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen40490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">some--</hi>the "scoffers."<div eID="gen40491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">count--</hi>His promise to be the result of "slackness" (tardiness).<div eID="gen40492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">long-suffering--</hi>waiting until the full number of those appointed to "salvation" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.15">2Pe 3:15</reference>) shall be completed.<div eID="gen40493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to us-ward--</hi>The oldest manuscripts, Vulgate, Syriac, &c., read, "towards YOU."<div eID="gen40494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">any--</hi>not desiring that any, yea, even that the scoffers, should perish, which would be the result if He did not give space for repentance.<div eID="gen40495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come--</hi>go and be received to repentance: the Greek implies there is room for their being received to repentance (compare Greek, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.2">Mr 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.37">Joh 8:37</reference>). <div eID="gen40496" type="x-p"/>
entries.195f8283152d6da207b2c6cc5210f4a6e2cc2647: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18884"/><div sID="gen40497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18884"/>10. The certainty, suddenness, and concomitant effects, of the coming of the day of the Lord. Faber argues from this that the millennium, &c., must precede Christ's literal coming, not follow it. But "the day of the Lord" comprehends the whole series of events, beginning with the pre-millennial advent, and ending with the destruction of the wicked, and final conflagration, and general judgment (which last intervenes between the conflagration and the renovation of the earth).<div eID="gen40497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will--</hi>emphatical. But (in spite of the mockers, and notwithstanding the delay) come and be present the day of the Lord SHALL.<div eID="gen40498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a thief--</hi>Peter remembers and repeats his Lord's image (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.39">Lu 12:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.41">41</reference>) used in the conversation in which he took a part; so also Paul (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.2">1Th 5:2</reference>) and John (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.3">Re 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.15">16:15</reference>).<div eID="gen40499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the heavens--</hi>which the scoffers say' shall "continue" as they are (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2Pe 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.35">Mt 24:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>).<div eID="gen40500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a great noise--</hi>with a rushing noise, like that of a whizzing arrow, or the crash of a devouring flame.<div eID="gen40501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">elements--</hi>the component materials of the world [Wahl]. However, as "the works" in the earth are mentioned separately from "the earth," so it is likely by "elements," mentioned after "the heavens," are meant "the works therein," namely, the sun, moon, and stars (as Theophilus of Antioch [p. 22, 148, 228]; and Justin Martyr [Apology, 2.44], use the word "elements"): these, as at creation, so in the destruction of the world, are mentioned [Bengel]. But as "elements" is not so used in Scripture Greek, perhaps it refers to the component materials of "the heavens," including the heavenly bodies; it clearly belongs to the former clause, "the heavens," not to the following, "the earth," &c.<div eID="gen40502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">melt--</hi>be dissolved, as in <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.11">2Pe 3:11</reference>.<div eID="gen40503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the works ... therein--</hi>of nature and of art. <div eID="gen40504" type="x-p"/>
entries.04aad811af902557b7488f2704b6044d5889feec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18885"/><div sID="gen40505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18885"/>11. Your duty, seeing that this is so, is to be ever eagerly expecting the day of God.<div eID="gen40505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>Some oldest manuscripts substitute "thus" for "then": a happy refutation of the "thus" of the scoffers, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2Pe 3:4</reference> (English Version, "As they were," Greek, "thus").<div eID="gen40506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be--</hi>Greek, "are being (in God's appointment, soon to be fulfilled) dissolved"; the present tense implying the certainty as though it were actually present.<div eID="gen40507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what manner of men--</hi>exclamatory. How watchful, prayerful, zealous!<div eID="gen40508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be--</hi>not the mere Greek substantive verb of existence (einai), but (huparchein) denoting a state or condition in which one is supposed to be [Tittmann]. What holy men ye ought to be found to be, when the event comes! This is "the holy commandment" mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.2">2Pe 3:2</reference>.<div eID="gen40509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">conversation ... godliness--</hi>Greek, plural: behaviors (towards men), godlinesses (or pieties towards God) in their manifold modes of manifestation. <div eID="gen40510" type="x-p"/>
entries.7de8485f9c40fbabe65bb422a46a1248366b7733: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18886"/><div sID="gen40511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18886"/><hi type="bold">12. hasting unto--</hi>with the utmost eagerness desiring [Wahl], praying for, and contemplating, the coming Saviour as at hand. The Greek may mean "hastening (that is, urging onward [Alford]) the day of God"; not that God's eternal appointment of the time is changeable, but God appoints us as instruments of accomplishing those events which must be first before the day of God can come. By praying for His coming, furthering the preaching of the Gospel for a witness to all nations, and bringing in those whom "the long-suffering of God" waits to save, we hasten the coming of the day of God. The Greek verb is always in New Testament used as neuter (as English Version here), not active; but the Septuagint uses it actively. Christ says, "Surely I come quickly. Amen." Our part is to speed forward this consummation by praying, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Re 22:20</reference>).<div eID="gen40511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the coming--</hi>Greek, "presence" of a person: usually, of the Saviour.<div eID="gen40512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day of God--</hi>God has given many myriads of days to men: one shall be the great "day of God" Himself.<div eID="gen40513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein--</hi>rather as Greek, "on account of (or owing to) which" day.<div eID="gen40514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavens--</hi>the upper and lower regions of the sky.<div eID="gen40515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40516" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">melt--</hi>Our igneous rocks show that they were once in a liquid state. <div eID="gen40516" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3dcd74cfbea9038c8cbe973617b767f0796204a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18887"/><div sID="gen40517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18887"/><hi type="bold">13. Nevertheless--</hi>"But": in contrast to the destructive effects of the day of God stand its constructive effects. As the flood was the baptism of the earth, eventuating in a renovated earth, partially delivered from "the curse," so the baptism with fire shall purify the earth so as to be the renovated abode of regenerated man, wholly freed from the curse.<div eID="gen40517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his promise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Is 65:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.22">66:22</reference>). The "we" is not emphatical as in English Version.<div eID="gen40518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new heavens--</hi>new atmospheric heavens surrounding the renovated earth.<div eID="gen40519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>dwelleth in that coming world as its essential feature, all pollutions having been removed. <div eID="gen40520" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2cdaf9aed485a6ae02478812ee5f98f2914b4d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18888"/><div sID="gen40521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18888"/><hi type="bold">14. that ye ... be found of him--</hi>"in His sight" [Alford], at His coming; plainly implying a personal coming.<div eID="gen40521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without spot--</hi>at the coming marriage feast of the Lamb, in contrast to <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.13">2Pe 2:13</reference>, "Spots they are and blemishes while they feast," not having on the King's pure wedding garment.<div eID="gen40522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blameless--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">1Co 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.10">Php 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">1Th 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">5:23</reference>).<div eID="gen40523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in peace--</hi>in all its aspects, towards God, your own consciences, and your fellow men, and as its consequence eternal blessedness: "the God of peace" will effect this for you. <div eID="gen40524" type="x-p"/>
